source.title: Advances in periodic difference equations with open problems

accepted.question_text: Let I be a compact interval in the real line, let p be a positive integer, and let f0, …, f_{p-1}: I → I generate the p-periodic non-autonomous system x_{n+1} = f_{n mod p}(x_n). Write Per([f0, …, f_{p-1}]) for the set of least periods of periodic orbits of this system. Characterize the possible sets Per([f0, …, f_{p-1}]) for arbitrary p, extending the exact period-forcing description known for 2-periodic systems.
accepted.context_brief: Periodic-orbit forcing for periodic interval systems

evidence.quote: For a fixed p ∈ N, consider a p-periodic system defined by the maps [f0, ..., fp−1].
Open Problem 2.1. Extend Theorem 2.1 to periodic sequences of maps of arbitrary period, i.e., characterize the set of periods Per([f0, ..., fp−1]) for any positive integer p.

accepted.question_text: In a p-periodic system [f0, …, f_{p-1}] of continuous interval maps, define A_{p,q} = {n : lcm(n, p) = q p}. Suppose some least period m of the system lies in A_{p,q}, where q > 1 is odd. Must the period p q also belong to Per([f0, …, f_{p-1}])? Prove that it must, or produce a counterexample.

evidence.quote: For q ∈ N, define the clusters Ap,q = {n : lcm(n, p) = q · p} = {n : q = n/gcd(n, p)}.
Open Problem 2.2. Suppose m ∈ Per([f0, ..., fp−1]) for some m ∈ Ap,q, where q > 1 is an odd number. Prove that pq ∈ Per([f0, ..., fp−1]).

accepted.question_text: Let f0, f1: S^1 → S^1 be continuous circle maps and consider the alternating system x_{n+1} = f_{n mod 2}(x_n). Characterize the set Per([f0, f1]) of least periods of periodic orbits for such 2-periodic systems on the circle, in the spirit of the interval result described by Theorem 2.1.

evidence.quote: Open Problem 2.3. Extend Theorem 2.1 to periodic sequences of two continuous circle maps, that is, characterize the set of periods Per([f0, f1]), where f0, f1 : S1 → S1 are continuous.

accepted.question_text: Let [f0, …, f_{p-1}] be a p-periodic system of continuous interval maps. For an integer k with 1 ≤ k ≤ p, form a folded system by composing blocks of k consecutive maps cyclically, producing maps F0, F1, … and hence a shorter-period system [F0, F1, …]. Determine the relationship between the set of least periods Per([f0, …, f_{p-1}]) of the original system and the set of least periods of the folded system.

evidence.quote: In general, for any 1 ≤ k ≤ p − 1, we can fold the maps fk−1 ◦ · · · ◦ f0 =: F0, f2k−1 ◦ · · · ◦ fk =: F1, f3k−1 ◦ · · · ◦ f2k =: F2, · · · to form another periodic system [F0, F1, ..., F p/gcd(p,k)].

Open Problem 3.1. Consider the p-periodic system [f0, ..., fp−1], and let 1 ≤ k ≤ p. Consider the maps F0, F1, . . . , F p/gcd(p,k) as defined in (3.1). What is the relationship between Per([f0, ..., fp−1]) and Per([F0, F1, ..., F p/gcd(p,k)])?

accepted.question_text: Suppose an unknown p-periodic system [f0, …, f_{p-1}] has a known folded system [F0, F1, …, F_{p/gcd(p,k)}]. Compare the periodic structure of the original unfolded system with the periodic structure of the delay equation x_{n+1} = F_n(x_{n-(k-1)}), where the index n is taken periodically through the folded maps. What similarity, if any, must these two systems have in their sets of periodic behaviors?

evidence.quote: From the columns of this matrix, observe that each column gives a periodic system of period p/gcd(p,k), which can be assumed to be the minimal period.

Open Problem 3.2. Suppose there is a p-periodic system [f0, ..., fp−1], which is unknown to us, but we know one of its folded systems [F0, F1, . . . , F p/gcd(p,k)]. What kind of similarity (if any) in periodic structure do we have between the unfolded p-periodic system [f0, ..., fp−1] and the periodic system with delay xn+1 = Fn(xn−(k−1))?

accepted.question_text: Let {a_n} and {b_n} be periodic sequences with least periods q1 and q2. Fix integers k1 and k2, and form a merged sequence by outputting k1 consecutive terms of {a_n}, then k2 consecutive terms of {b_n}, and repeating this process indefinitely. Determine the minimal period of the merged sequence in full generality, without assuming that the two original sequences are disjoint.
accepted.context_brief: Minimal period of merged periodic sequences

evidence.quote: Suppose we have two periodic sequences {an} and {bn} of periods q1 and q2, respectively. ... The obtained signal has the structure [an, bn] := a1, a2, . . . , ak1, b1, b2, . . . , bk2, ak1+1, ak1+2, . . .
Open Problem 4.1. For n ∈ N, let {an} and {bn} be two periodic sequences of periods q1 and q2, respectively. Find the minimal period of the sequence [an, bn] formed in (4.1).

accepted.question_text: If f0 and f1 are commuting continuous self-maps of a compact interval I, must they share a periodic point? Equivalently, is the intersection P(f0) ∩ P(f1) necessarily nonempty, where P(f) denotes the set of periodic points of f?
accepted.context_brief: Common periodic points for commuting interval maps

evidence.quote: Denote by Fix(f) and P(f) the set of fixed and periodic points of a map f ∈ C(I), respectively. We consider two maps f0, f1 ∈ C(I) such that they commute, that is, f0 ◦ f1 = f1 ◦ f0.
Open Problem 5.1. Is it true that P(f0) ∩ P(f1) 6= ∅ for commuting continuous interval maps f0, f1 ∈ C(I)?

accepted.question_text: For commuting continuous interval maps f0, f1: I → I, determine the set Per([f0, f1]) of least periods of periodic orbits of the alternating system x_{n+1} = f_{n mod 2}(x_n). In particular, decide whether every period pattern realized by the noncommuting examples from Theorem 2.1 can also be realized by a commuting pair.

evidence.quote: Open Problem 5.2. Find Per([f0, f1]) for commuting maps f0, f1 ∈ C(I). More precisely, can the examples of Theorem 2.1 be constructed such that f0 and f1 commute?

accepted.question_text: For a continuous interval map f, let D(f) denote its collection of dynamical properties, and call a property P an L-property if P is preserved when f is restricted to a compact subinterval and linearly rescaled back to [0, 1] in the sense described in the paper. Given three L-properties P1, P2, and P3, prove or disprove that there exist commuting maps f0, f1: [0, 1] → [0, 1] such that f0 has property P1, f1 has property P2, and the composition f0 ∘ f1 has property P3.

evidence.quote: For a map f ∈ C(I), I = [0, 1], denote by D(f) the set of dynamic properties of f ... A dynamic property P ∈ D(f) is an L–property if for any continuous map f and any compact subinterval J ⊆ [0, 1], it is held that P ∈ D(f) ∩ D(fJ ).
Theorem 6.1. Let Pi, i = 1, 2, 3, be L–properties. Then there are f0, f1 ∈ C(I) such that P1 ∈ D(f0), P2 ∈ D(f1) and P3 ∈ D(f0 ◦ f1).
Open Problem 6.1. State an analogous result to Theorem 6.1 when the maps f0 and f1 commute.

accepted.question_text: For the logistic family fa(x) = a x(1 − x) on [0, 1] with parameters a ∈ [1, 4], characterize the pairs (a, b) such that every finite composition built from fa and fb exhibits the dynamic Parrondo paradox, meaning that the combined dynamics has the paradoxical complexity behavior discussed in the paper rather than behaving like the individual maps. Is the set of such parameter pairs nonempty?

evidence.quote: Parrondo’s paradox exists when the behavior of individual systems and the combined one are completely different. For discrete dynamical systems, the paradox was formulated in [4] by showing that the phenomenon “chaos+chaos=order” and “order+order=chaos” are possible when considering periodic combinations of 1-dimensional quadratic maps.
Open Problem 6.2. Characterize the set of parameters a, b ∈ [1, 4] such that any combination of maps fa and fb exhibit the Parrondo’s paradox. Is this set nonempty?

accepted.question_text: Let fa(x) = a x(1 − x) and fb(x) = b x(1 − x) be logistic maps on [0, 1], and let h(f) denote topological entropy. Prove or disprove the implication min(h(fa), h(fb)) > 0 ⇒ h(fa ∘ fb) > 0.
accepted.context_brief: Entropy under composition of logistic maps

evidence.quote: Denote the topological entropy of a continuous map f by h(f).
Open Problem 6.3. In the logistic family, prove or disprove that min{h(fa), h(fb)} > 0 implies that h(fa ◦ fb) > 0.

accepted.question_text: Consider the periodically forced stocking model x_{n+1} = x_n f(x_n) + h_n, where {h_n} is a p-periodic sequence of stocking quotas, and assume the system has a global attractor. If {ĥ_n} is a permutation of the same quota multiset, and x_av and ĥx_av denote the averages of the corresponding global attractors, how is x_av related to ĥx_av?

evidence.quote: Forcing periodic harvesting or stocking in a deterministic environment leads to investigating the dynamics of models in the form xn+1 = xnf(xn) ± hn, where {hn} is a p-periodic sequence that represents harvesting or stocking quotas.

Open Problem 7.1. Consider Eq. (7.1) with stocking (i.e. +hn) and assume this equation has a global attractor ... Let {hˆn} be a permutation of {hn}. Define xav and xˆav to be the average of the global attractors associated with {hn} and {hˆn}, respectively. How does xav relate to xˆav?

accepted.question_text: Consider the periodically forced harvesting model x_{n+1} = x_n f(x_n) − h_n, where {h_n} is a periodic sequence of harvesting quotas. If one is free to permute the order of the quotas while keeping the same multiset of values, which permutation is most favorable to the population, both in terms of enlarging the basin of attraction and in terms of maximizing the arithmetic average of the attractor?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 7.2. Consider Eq. (7.1) with harvesting (i.e. −hn). Investigate the effect of ordering the elements of the sequence {hn} on the population. On other words, assume that we have a periodic sequence of harvesting quotas but we have the freedom to permute its elements. Which permutation of {hn} plays on the advantage of the population in terms of the basin of attraction and in terms of the arithmetic average of the attractor?
